entries.title: James Talarico’s Campaign Is Refunding Over $1 Million in Excess Contributions
entries.summary: Federal regulators keep flagging donors to the Texas Democrat who gave over the legal limit.
entries.content:
James Talarico keeps raising too much money.

The Texas Democrat has already raised more than $70 million in his bid to defeat state Attorney General Ken Paxton for U.S. Senate — more than any other non-incumbent candidate has raised this cycle nationwide and millions more than his Republican rival has amassed.

But scores of Talarico donors are exceeding federal donation limits, with regulators at the Federal Election Commission identifying 143 such donors who exceeded the legal limit, according to a 24-page letter they sent to the Talarico campaign this month.

It’s not the first time Talarico, who is attempting to become the first Texas Democrat elected to statewide office since 1994, has received such a missive: Every quarter since its inception, Talarico for Texas has received warnings about accepting donations beyond the legal limit.

The campaign, in turn, has to date reported 534 refunds totaling $844,347. Another quarter-million dollars or so worth of refunds or reattributions are expected after the FEC’s latest letter.
https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/fX0XQ/1/https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/8Fx5w/1/Among the flagged Talarico donors is Colorado Gov. Jared Polis, who made two donations in March for $2,000 and $2,500 designated for the general election — $1,000 over the legal limit. (Polis’ office did not respond to a request for comment.)

One of the largest reported contributions came from Robert E. Price, the son of Sol Price, who founded the companies that would become Costco. He donated a lump sum of $14,000 to Talarico’s campaign, well above the federal limit.

Unlike Price, many of the donors who exceeded the FEC limit on contributions didn’t make a single large contribution. Rather, their small-dollar donations added up to more than the $3,500 individuals are allowed to give per election.

Sharon Freeto, a retiree from San Antonio, had 20 of her Talarico campaign contributions flagged this month by the FEC for giving over the contribution limit — 10 of which were made on April 24, according to federal records.

“I have no memory of how that happened. That's a lot of money,” Freeto said of the April transactions. She added that she agreed to make monthly donations to the campaign.

Freeto said she had already received a refund for some of her contributions.

“I got a check for the $1,000 refunded with a suggestion to sign it over to, I think it was the national Democratic Party,” she told NOTUS. (The Democratic National Committee began the summer in debt, while the Republican National Committee boasted about $125 million in reserve.)

Even as it came as a surprise, Freeto said she wasn’t too concerned about the transactions.

“I would have missed that if I hadn’t done it,” she said, laughing, adding that this is the first time she had “given so much” to a candidate.

“Two things came together at the same time,” Freeto said. “One is that I really believe in this candidate — I really believe in James Talarico — and the other thing is that for the first time in my life, I have spare money.” She said she supports Talarico because he is the “ideal candidate” for people like her, a self-proclaimed liberal Democrat.

In an emailed statement to NOTUS, the Talarico campaign said its web address used to send financial contributions is automatically set to “donate once to avoid donors automatically being signed up to make monthly donations if they’re unaware of it.” 

A second donor flagged by the FEC for contributing $10,000 to the campaign told NOTUS that he contributed the maximum amount of $3,500 to the campaign, with the rest of the lump sum going to a different entity.

“I was told $3,500 was the max I could contribute to the campaign and that the excess would be reallocated to what I thought to some entity associated with the Democratic Party in Texas,” he said when asked for more details about his contribution. He declined to answer more questions over the phone.

The Talarico campaign explained that a donor who makes an excess contribution “will receive a check in the mail with the difference in their donation that has exceeded the donation limit to Talarico for Texas, as well as a letter explaining we are returning their money and sharing ideas as to where they can donate to if they wish to donate it to a similar cause.”

Issue One, a “crosspartisan” nonprofit organization that seeks to reduce the influence of money in politics, said in a statement to NOTUS that the Talarico campaign is both “following the law and trying to do what is right by proactively communicating with donors about excess campaign contributions.”

“Congress needs to create a campaign finance system that is more transparent, accountable, and understandable to the American public,” said Alix Fraser, vice president of advocacy for Issue One. “Issues like excess contributions plague Democrats and Republicans alike and show why our country needs sweeping anti-corruption legislation.”

It’s not uncommon for big-dollar Senate or presidential candidates to allow some excessive donations to slip through. Regulators said 17 donors recently made excessive contributions to Ken Paxton for Senate.

“Federal regulations allow 60 days to resolve an excess contribution,” Madison Cercy, the Paxton campaign’s deputy director of communications, told NOTUS in a statement. “The Candidate Committee, and all associated Joint Fundraising Committee's strive to maintain compliance with the 60-day rule and have done so.”

But Talarico’s campaign is notable for how much money it’s had to give back amid its endless quest for election-season cash.

Both campaigns send a torrent of near-daily fundraising emails. It’s gotten to the point that Talarico’s subject lines make light of the fire hose of solicitations: “I apologize for invading your inbox,” “Sorry to ask” and just simply “Sorry.”
KenPaxton (2711x1808, AR: 1.50)The Paxton campaign, fresh from a bruising and expensive primary election in which Paxton defeated Sen. John Cornyn, has taken every opportunity to highlight his own fundraising struggles in emails to potential donors with subject lines that underscore the severity of his shortfall:

“Outraised by over 300%.”

“We just saw Talarico's May numbers. This is bad.”

“I won’t lie to you… This is bad.”

“This is bad. Very bad!”

In his own fundraising pitches, Talarico largely overlooks Paxton’s dismal numbers — the Republican has fewer than $2 million on hand in his campaign account — instead focusing on the hundreds of millions of dollars amassed by Paxton-aligned super PACs Senate Leadership Fund and MAGA Inc. The latter is reportedly preparing to spend significant money to aid Paxton.

“Our state is being taken over by a new kind of tyrant: billionaire mega-donors,” Talarico wrote in a recent fundraising pitch. “Grassroots donations are our best chance to level the playing field.”

“We cannot let the tyrants win.”

entries.title: Germany's Far-Right Is On the Rise. The Implications Are Global.
entries.summary: Eight decades after the Nazis fell, the AfD is poised to win a leadership role that could forever alter governing in the European country.
entries.content:
BERLIN — In a few weeks, Germany’s far-right party — Alternative for Germany, better known as AfD — could become a governing party of a German state for the first time. The stakes go far beyond the one state — and likely beyond Europe.

Germany’s modern political system was designed to prevent far-right rule. But Ulrich Siegmund, AfD’s head candidate, is currently leading in polls to become the head of a state government, Saxony-Anhalt.

The Sept. 6 election has the AfD candidates polling significantly better than in previous elections. Should there be a state-level win in Saxony-Anhalt, the change could build momentum for high AfD turnout across Germany later in September.

An AfD win in one state “signals to other elections that are coming up that it's possible for them to win,” according to Lukas Stöetzer, a political science professor at the University of Witten/Herdecke. “It would give [the AfD] a small boost.”

A far-right rise in Germany — the European Union’s largest economy and a strategic pillar of NATO — could have lasting global effects. If the AfD increases its influence in the federal government, it could dial back support for Ukraine’s defense against Russia and adopt a warmer posture toward Vladimir Putin’s country, both moves that most Western leaders don’t support.

The government in Germany operates much differently than its American counterpart. In Germany, state governments control votes in the Bundesrat, the federal upper house representing the states that approves federal legislation. An AfD-led state government would have a major impact on how the Bundesrat governs and for the Christian Democratic Union of Germany, the country’s leading center-right political party.

AfD's rise is the latest chapter in a broader far-right surge across Europe, from Giorgia Meloni's premiership in Italy to Marine Le Pen's National Rally emerging as France's leading opposition force. But not every far-right party endorses AfD's approach: Le Pen has publicly distanced herself from the AfD's methods and rhetoric.

In Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD is leading the polls, with support at roughly 41%, about 20 points ahead of the CDU — a lead wide enough that the party could govern alone outright if smaller parties like the center-left Social Democrats fail to clear Germany's 5% threshold for parliamentary representation.

Siegmund, the AfD candidate, is media-savvy and has a large internet following. He’s served in the Landtag, or state parliament, of Saxony-Anhalt since 2016 and has been co-group leader of the AfD faction there since 2022. He has cited ending migration to Germany and prioritizing “remigration,” or deportation of immigrants, as important issues.

But for about a decade, Germany’s mainstream parties have had an informal but strictly enforced political consensus, called Brandmauer, to never cooperate with the AfD. That could all change after Sept. 6.

Experts have pointed to a clear divide between East and West Germany that never fully recovered after the Berlin Wall fell, with East Germany struggling with issues similar to many regions of the United States: industrial job loss, rising prices and unemployment, and an influx of migrants.

“We have a special problem in the Eastern states …because of the crisis after unification, especially economic affairs,” said Hajo Funke, a retired political science professor who worked at the Free University of Berlin. “This has had traumatic [effects], be it the high unemployment, especially soon after unification and lack of comparable well-being like in West Germany.”

“We have a party, the right-wingish, racist, extremist AfD, who built upon [dissatisfaction in Germany] and tried to get executive functions in Saxon-Anhalt,” he added.

Some Germans' concerns about AfD center on the party's purported neo-Nazi connections, anti-immigrant policies and rhetoric that romanticizes Germany's past. Notably, Saxony-Anhalt's AfD state branch has been formally classified as “confirmed right-wing extremist" by Germany's domestic intelligence agency (Verfassungsschutz) since 2023.

“Björn Höcke is leaning to neo-Nazi ideas and he’s very influential, maybe the most influential within the party,” Funke said, speaking about the AfD leader in Thuringia, a German state.

Berlin votes on Sept. 20, just two weeks later, and AfD candidates are also leading in the polls there for the first time, making it a "double test" rather than an isolated event.

Germany’s current government makeup is a coalition of the CDU and the Social Democratic Party of Germany, led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz, formed after the February 2025 federal election that ousted former Chancellor Olaf Scholz's government.

entries.title: Start Your Engines
entries.content:
Good morning. This is the NOTUS Metro newsletter for Aug. 17, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!


THE LATEST

It’s off to the races this weekend as the Freedom 250 Grand Prix roars into D.C., the final stop in a long summer of local disruptions around the nation’s 250th birthday celebrations.

The disturbances include a host of road closures near the racecourse — which loops around the National Mall — that are already diverting bus routes and will modify access to courts and museums.

Thirteen bus routes will be detoured by the race. Some are scheduled to be affected until Sept. 15, more than three weeks after the race is over, though that could change if roads reopen sooner. D.C.’s Department of Transportation didn’t respond to a request for comment there.

D.C. Courts will remain open this week, but Bankruptcy Court hearings will be remote. Anyone coming to court in person is advised to factor in additional time for commuting and prepare for security checkpoints related to the race.

Access to three Smithsonian museums will be restricted. On Friday, anyone can visit the Air and Space, American Indian and Natural History museums — though you’ll need to get a pass, and will need to go through metal detectors at the Grand Prix entrances. Over the weekend, though, only visitors with Grand Prix tickets will be able to get into those museums.

Want a ticket? Free general admission tickets are no longer available. Premium tickets are still available through the “Freedom 250 Grand Champions Club.” But the weekend package, which offers all-inclusive food and drinks, costs just over $5,000. Single-day Champions Club tickets can be had on Ticketmaster for closer to $3,500 as of Sunday.





DEEP DIVE

Faith Ngwa is one of hundreds of thousands of college freshmen who will move into their first dorm room this month. But the Hagerstown native will begin college coming off a summer full of uncertainty and panic. Only a few weeks ago, she wasn’t sure if she’d make it to move-in day. That’s because she was one of about 500 incoming Howard University students who were unenrolled in July over payment issues.

After her account was reexamined, Ngwa was reenrolled. But the whirlwind, weeklong experience left her with mixed emotions. NOTUS’ Shamira Muhammad joined Ngwa and her family on campus as they got settled. The teenager felt proud to be a new Bison, but also cautious about the future. More than anything, she is determined to make the most of the next four years.

“I do want to run for a lot of things, join a lot of organizations,” she said. “Because hey, if Howard has already stressed me out this much, I might as well take full advantage.” 

DSC04182 copy.jpg (3504x2336, AR: 1.50)




FROM THE DISTRICT

A woman accused of vandalizing the World War II Memorial in D.C. last week is facing two felony charges of depredation against property of the United States and destruction of veterans' memorials. Prosecutors allege that Melissa Farris of Kentucky spray painted the memorial and filled a fountain with dishwasher detergent. “Defacing the World War II Memorial is a disgusting act and an insult to the Americans who fought and died for our country,” U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jeanine Pirro wrote in a social media post.

Changes at Reagan National Airport in the wake of the deadly January 2025 crash between a commercial airliner and a military helicopter have been slow in coming, reports The Washington Post. Of 52 recommendations made by the National Transportation Safety Board to prevent future crashes, 51 remain open.

A Michelin-starred restaurant in Shaw is facing eviction over more than $183,000 in unpaid rent dating back to March, the Washington Business Journal reports. Mita, a Latin American restaurant in Northwest D.C., was sued last month by an affiliate of JBG Smith, its landlord.

JBG Smith — a real estate investment trust with a massive footprint in the DMV — is in financial trouble of its own, with about $2.6 billion in debt and a reported 12 straight quarters of losses. NOTUS previously reported on abysmal conditions at another property it co-owns: The Gale Eckington.

The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on Friday to greenlight the president’s $400 million White House ballroom project, arguing in part that the safety of the president is at stake, NOTUS’ Ben T.N. Mause reports.

How do you like them apples? About 1,000 people gathered at Malcolm X Park on Saturday to eat an apple together, The Post reports.





D.C. TRIVIA


Where was the last place car racing was held in D.C.?

  1. RFK Stadium
  2. East Potomac Park
  3. Audi Field
Email us the answer — the first reader who gets it right gets a shout-out. The answer will be at the end of the newsletter tomorrow.





SPORTS

The Commanders are 1-0. Well, 1-0 in the preseason. Washington beat Miami on Friday in the first of its three preseason games, a 20-7 victory that served as a showcase of the team’s depth. NOTUS’ Martenzie Johnson reports that the game’s standouts included an undrafted running back and a former Terp on the defensive line.

Quarterback Marcus Mariota is expected to miss the rest of the preseason after he hobbled off with an injury midway through the first quarter Friday night. ESPN reports that the veteran backup has a sprained MCL.

Mystics legends Chamique Holdsclaw and Elena Delle Donne were inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame over the weekend. Delle Donne played in Washington for six years, leading the Mystics to a WNBA title in 2019. The franchise took Holdsclaw No. 1 overall in 1999, and she also spent six seasons in D.C.





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@notus.com.

The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson. Photo by Lillian Bautista/NOTUS.

entries.title: Day 269
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Trump faces backlash over deployment comments. The Body Guy Caucus. Lawmakers vs. “The Donroe Doctrine.” James Talarico’s overmaxed donors. The NIH’s grant holdup. And: A far-right party on the rise in Germany.

THE LATEST

It’s day 269 of the USS Abraham Lincoln’s record-breaking deployment that has service members' families worried about their well-being. President Donald Trump responded to a question about that concern by saying the deployment hasn’t gone on “nearly long enough.”

Trump ordered the U.S. joint military exercises with South Korea — which start today — to be substantially reduced, not only because they are costly but also because they “send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile” to North Korea and, as the president put it, “somewhat unrelated (?)” because South Korea didn’t lend a hand with Iran.

Trump’s support among military ranks has been strong since his first election, according to polling earlier this year, but his moves are fresh fodder for those who say he’s dismissive of Americans serving in uniform.

“For a guy who called those who put their lives on the line ‘suckers’ and ‘losers,’ these latest comments are consistent,” retired Army Gen. Paul Eaton, a senior adviser to the progressive group VoteVets, told us. “It just keeps sending the message that he doesn't respect or even grasp all our troops and military families have given and continue to give. How much it hurts recruiting and retention, I can’t say. I can say it doesn’t help.”

“The response of the president of the United States pisses me off. And it should piss all of us off,” Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, a Democrat and a U.S. Army veteran, told CNN yesterday. “We are continuing to fight this foreign forever war for a commander-in-chief who seems to have not one modicum of concern for the people who are out there fighting it.”

Relief appears to be on the way for the USS Abraham Lincoln and its 5,000 sailors and Marines, with the USS George Washington en route to replace it.

Adm. Brad Cooper, the head of U.S. Central Command, visited the Lincoln over the weekend and described his time aboard the aircraft carrier as “awe-inspiring,” adding that the ship reports the “lowest number of cases related to mental health” of the Navy’s 11 active aircraft carriers.

“To all our Sailors and Marines aboard the ship,” the admiral said, “keep up the great work and fair winds and following seas on the journey home.”

Open tabs: AIPAC Targets Progressive Democrat in Race to Replace Swalwell (NYT); Hamas leaders tell Kushner they will demilitarize Gaza, sources say (Axios); Crowley leads Tiffany by four points in new head-to-head poll of likely voters (WPR); Trump turns to containing the fallout from setbacks in Iran (LAT)


From the Hill


It’s called the “Body Guy Caucus,” though some are women. NOTUS’ Hill team goes inside the strange and often silly world of the most secretive aides in the Senate: the people who follow senators around, and maybe know their ATM PINs. All are required to wear many hats, including valet, scheduler, traffic cop and sometimes even emotional support animal. One describes having to carry around a false tooth that had fallen out of their boss’ mouth. “It is literally Gary from ‘Veep,’” one former body person said. “It is the most accurate description of the job that we do.”

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) says his body guy, Lee Dudley, is essential. But other senators pointedly do not have one. “I'd rather be alone, not have a tagalong. I'm also one of those people who has personal space, and I know that I need more personal space than a lot of Easterners do,” said Sen. Cynthia Lummis (R-Wyoming).

Regional leftists vs. “The Donroe Doctrine:” Rep. Pramila Jayapal and 10 other like-minded U.S. lawmakers blasted Trump’s foreign policy interventions in the Western Hemisphere ahead of the Panamerican Congress, a gathering of progressive legislators from across the two continents, NOTUS’ Akbar Shahid Ahmed tells us. The American lawmakers urged “respect for sovereignty” in a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

From the campaign trail


Following the money: James Talarico’s megadonors. Scores of donors for the Democratic nominee for Senate in Texas are exceeding federal donation limits, with regulators at the FEC recently identifying 143 such donors who gave more than the maximum allowed, NOTUS’ Torrie Herrington and Mark Alfred report. Every quarter since the campaign’s inception, the FEC has flagged this problem — and the campaign has responded with a reported 534 refunds totaling more than $840,000. Another quarter-million dollars or so worth of refunds or reattributions are expected.

Many of the donors who exceeded the FEC limit on contributions didn’t make a single large contribution. Rather, their small-dollar donations added up to more than the $3,500 cap. “I got a check for the $1,000 refunded with a suggestion to sign it over to, I think it was the national Democratic Party,” one donor, a retired woman from San Antonio, told NOTUS. She’s had 20 of her donations to Talarico flagged as exceeding the legal limits.

From HHS

NIH’s “graveyard for grants:” Doling out federal grant money is a key responsibility of the National Institutes of Health. And, as you may imagine, there is a dizzying amount of red tape required: editing and review steps, peer review and a second look by an advisory council — often due to federal statute. But in Trump 2.0, a new hurdle has emerged, NOTUS’ Paige Winfield Cunningham reports.

Status 19 — an administrative code describing awards with senior leadership sign-off — is being used as the holding cell for grants as they undergo extra political review. Internal grant review documents that Paige obtained show officials flagged words including “diverse,” “equity,” “structural” and “underrepresented,” and asked for more clarification in projects that focused on health disparities or racial groups.

The reviews are holding many grants — and grant renewals — in political limbo. NIH disputes that. A spokesperson said grants can remain in Status 19 for five to 10 days while they are given final review by the Office of Extramural Research. “There is no political appointee review stage in the NIH grant review process,” the spokesperson said in a statement. 

NOTUS METRO

Sign up for our local newsletter, written by Martin Austermuhle and Zara Norman.

Local news: After a Summer of Uncertainty and Panic, a Howard Freshman Moves In, by Shamira Muhammad

Sports desk: Five Takeaways From the Commanders’ Preseason Win Over the Dolphins, by Martenzie Johnson


NEW ON NOTUS

A far-right party is on the rise in Germany, and it could have lasting global effects. Ulrich Siegmund, a candidate for Alternative for Germany (known as AfD), is currently leading in polls to become the head of government in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, NOTUS’ Daniella Diaz reports from Berlin. An AfD win in one state “signals to other elections that are coming up that it's possible for them to win,” according to Lukas Stöetzer, a political science professor at the University of Witten/Herdecke.

Germany’s modern political system was designed to prevent far-right rule — with the country’s mainstream parties generally disavowing coalition building with the AfD. The country has the European Union’s largest economy and is a strategic pillar of NATO, but the AfD could dial back Germany’s support for Ukraine’s defense against Russia.

More: Ken Martin Is Open to Change at the DNC, by Alex Roarty and Elena Schneider

Data Centers Are Defining the Wisconsin Governor’s Race, by Marissa Martinez

Trump Administration Greenlights World Liberty Financial Bank Charter, Jade Lozada

Blanche Says DOJ Could Take Voter Roll Fight to the Supreme Court, by Jenna Monnin

NOT US

  • Democrats Face a Potential Tea Party Moment, by Lisa Lerer and Katie Glueck for The New York Times
  • Republicans are attacking Democrats as vegans on the campaign trail, by Samuel Benson for Politico
  • How Trump Left America Vulnerable to Cyberattacks, by Nick Miroff and Yvonne Wingett Sanchez for The Atlantic

WEEK AHEAD

Tuesday 

Primary day in Alaska, Florida and Wyoming.

Special election in California’s 14th Congressional District to replace former Rep. Eric Swalwell.

Sen. Darline Graham and Rep. Ralph Norman debate ahead of the Aug. 25 Republican Senate runoff in South Carolina.

Thursday 

Democratic Senate primary debate in Massachusetts.

Hearing in the case of Cole Allen, the suspect in the shooting at the April 25 White House Correspondents’ Association dinner.

entries.title: ‘Graveyard for Grants’: NIH Is Holding Up Medical Research Funding
entries.summary: Hundreds of grants, including for maternal health, contraceptives and drug abuse, are in limbo, subject to political reviews.
entries.content:
It used to be that once a National Institutes of Health grant award hit “status 19,” the money was about to go out the door.

That’s not the case anymore. The Trump administration has enacted an unprecedented political review process, pushing hundreds of awards into limbo. Status 19 — an administrative code describing awards with senior leadership sign-off — is being used as the holding cell.

Current and former career staff say this extra review by senior leaders is occurring after grants have undergone peer review, been approved by multiple offices in NIH, and screened for red-flag words around race, gender or other behavioral and social sciences. The extra political reviews are required not only for newly funded grants but also for annual payment installments for previously awarded projects.

As a result, some grants are lingering in status 19 for weeks or even months, gumming up the works as grant officers try to get awards out the door ahead of the new fiscal year starting in October. Flagged grants reviewed by NOTUS had to do with maternal health, contraceptive use, aging, dementia and opioid abuse.

“The notion that Francis Collins or Mike Lauer would ever have reviewed individual grants like this is so beyond the realm of comprehension,” a senior career staffer said, referring to the former directors of NIH and its Office of Extramural Research. “It’s laughable to me.”

A second senior NIH official called status 19 a “graveyard for grants.” The NIH staffers were granted anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak to the media.

As one of the largest grant funders in the federal government, NIH’s process is a prime example of how the Trump administration is implementing more political oversight of grants across a wide swath of agencies, even as its efforts to formalize those reviews face pushback.

Senate Republicans voted to temporarily block a White House regulation to formalize political review, which has already led to delays in posting and awarding grants at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, the Department of Interior and other agencies.

Researchers, patient advocates and biotech companies are outraged by the proposed regulation, which the White House is seeking to implement by Oct. 1 but could be blocked until December if the House also approves a delay.

Senior NIH leaders sent around a new agency review flowchart in May outlining additional steps once an award hits status 19. The flowchart, viewed by NOTUS, mandates a review by the NIH Office of Extramural Research (OER) and an HHS counselor before grantees are given a notice of award. There are no political appointees at OER, but its director reports to NIH Director and Trump appointee Jay Bhattacharya.

As a result of the extra reviews, the number of grants sitting for weeks in status 19 have surged. Around 8% of new grant awards are sitting in status 19 for anywhere from two to seven weeks, according to internal data shared with NOTUS.

In past years, around 11% of first-time awards had been released to the recipients within a week. This year, it’s 2%.

The delays are even more pronounced for annual payment installments for ongoing grants. The vast majority previously left status 19 within three days; now it takes 53 days to get 90% of payments out the door.

Lauer, who served as NIH’s extramural research director from 2015 to February 2025, said he couldn’t recall a time when a political appointee — including the NIH director — halted awarding of a research grant after it had gone through the review and approval process.

“Status 19 was not something I thought about,” Lauer told NOTUS.

NIH career staff stress that by the time grant awards reach status 19, they have been through dozens of editing and review steps. They’ve undergone peer review and a second look by an advisory council. Grant officers have gone through a checklist, including confirming that women and racial minorities have been appropriately included, something required by statute.

In grants reviewed by NOTUS, HHS or EOR staff flagged words including “diverse,” “equity,” “structural” and “underrepresented” and asked for clarification about what the researchers meant by them. In one project, a staffer wrote that the word “structural” could include concepts that are inconsistent with NIH priorities.

They asked for more clarification in projects that focused on health disparities or racial groups. Officials wrote that focusing on specific racial groups required more justification. In one project that expressed support for scholars and researchers from a variety of backgrounds, an official responded that the language could raise legal concerns if interpreted as targeting people based on demographics.

In multiple flagged grants, officials expressed concerns that they weren’t worth funding because their only practical use might be to support the writing of new laws.

HHS spokeswoman Emily Hilliard disputed the notion that status 19 is being used to hold up grants under extra political reviews. She said grants can remain in status 19 for five to 10 days while they are given final review by the Office of Extramural Research.

“There is no political appointee review stage in the NIH grant review process,” Hilliard said in a statement. “OER's review is a longstanding part of NIH’s grant review process.”

Lauer said releasing grant money might face occasional delays, but it was almost always because Congress had failed to pass a budget for NIH, leading to uncertainty about how much total grant funding would be available.

Trump appointees are also conducting extra layers of review to the notices posted by the government to let researchers know money is available for specific projects or programs. Researchers say they’ve seen more delays in posting those notices — another obstacle in getting grant funding out the door.

“It’s this black box of HHS review,” said Colleen Kelley, an associate dean for research at Emory University.

entries.title: The 'Body Guy Caucus': The Lives of the Men and Women Paid to Shadow Senators
entries.summary: The job is part babysitter, part confidante and sometimes part purse-holder. But body people are essential to making the place work, senators say.
entries.content:
There's a secretive cadre of young staffers whose job it is to make the Senate run more efficiently. They’re known informally as the “Body Guy Caucus,” though some are women.

They can be found by most senators’ sides, helping them navigate the maze of hallways, tunnels and subways in the Capitol complex as well as the crowds of reporters outside the Senate chamber who are eager to pounce on their bosses for a quote.

While most congressional staffers tend to work out of an office, body people spend nearly every waking hour shadowing their boss, performing a unique set of duties that include valet, scheduler, traffic cop and sometimes even emotional support animal. It’s a position of trust many senators take very seriously, and one that comes with a high level of stress.

“It is the craziest position to have on the Hill, and it is the best position to have on the Hill, because you have these 22-year-olds that are more or less babysitting some of the most important and powerful people in the country,” one former body person told NOTUS.

Body people are sometimes tasked with oddball personal requests, too, like random household tasks, grocery shopping and walking dogs. The body person for one Democratic senator was once dispatched to buy their boss nylons. Another former body person recalled once having to safekeep an envelope containing their boss’s false tooth that fell out during the workday.
U.S. Congress (5000x3333, AR: 1.50)Admittedly, getting a body person to talk is a challenge. Given the sensitive nature of the job, they aren’t supposed to speak with the press. And unlike other roles in Congress that can be highly competitive and partisan, body people tend to look out for each other — regardless of party affiliation. So when we began reaching out to them, many were already aware that reporters were snooping around, having been tipped off by their fellow body guys and gals.

“Everyone supports one another since they are the only people to really understand what everyone goes through with the long hours and requirements of the job. It’s a microcosm of the Senate,” one body guy told NOTUS.

Most body people tend to be right out of college, using the job as a stepping stone to gain skills and build a network as they work their way up the Capitol Hill ladder. Some have even risen to the coveted role of chief of staff.

Body people spend so much time with their boss, they can pick up their idiosyncrasies. Sen. Katie Britt’s (R-Alabama) body person, for example, wears tennis shoes similar to Britt’s to keep up with one of the fastest lawmakers on Capitol Hill. The body guy for Sen. John Kennedy (R-Louisiana) — one of the Hill’s most accessible and loquacious senators — has heard his boss speak so much, he’s begun talking like him and even uses some of his famous one-liners.
bagperson.jpg (3000x2000, AR: 1.50)bodyguys.jpg (5680x3787, AR: 1.50)“It is literally Gary from ‘Veep.’ … It is the most accurate description of the job that we do,” the first former body person said, referring to the HBO show that depicts a vice president’s devoted body man enduring verbal abuse and lots of emotional distress. The show is widely considered the most spot-on TV representation of life in Washington, D.C.

The role of body man in the Senate isn’t new, though it’s become more common in recent years, especially with the arrival of more media-shy members who aren’t accustomed to the likes of TMZ and other outlets pointing cameras in their face.

In the 1990s, young staffers typically began their careers working as drivers for members and, with that proximity to their bosses, often soared up the ranks in the Capitol for no other reason than the trust they gained in the process.

The modern role largely originated with former Texas Sen. Kay Bailey Hutchison’s group of rotating young male aides, nicknamed “purse boys,” who were tasked with carrying her handbag around the Capitol. At any given time, Hutchison had two individuals fill the role, allowing them to switch out driving and walking with her in the halls.

“She famously had an entourage,” Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), who served alongside the ex-senator, said with a big smile. He noted that his own chief of staff, Drew Brandewie, once held that position for Hutchison.

The tradition isn’t dead, either. At a recent vote in the Senate, a male aide was spotted trailing behind Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-Tennessee), purse in hand.

The needs of members have bred all variations of who they wander the hallways with. Senate Majority Leader John Thune did not have a dedicated body person until he took on the top spot of the conference.
Sen. John Hoeven,lefta and Sen. John Kennedy,center. (5140x3427, AR: 1.50)Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) can commonly be seen with three people at any given time: his body person, a policy or press advisor depending on where he’s going, plus a security aide.

“The body man's one of the most important roles in politics,” Cruz told NOTUS, noting that he tends to hire older-than-usual body men since he views it as such a crucial role. “A good body man makes you a thousand times more effective. A lousy body man ensures constant problems and constant obstacles in the way to accomplishing your work.”

“My body men are also a portal to the entire rest of the team,” Cruz added, pointing to Lee Dudley, his body man. “As you can see, he's recording this conversation. When it's over, he will send it to the press team. If I broke some pressing news on national security policy, he'd make sure the national security policy people saw it.”

Dudley described his job succinctly.

“You wear many different hats,” he said.

On the other end of the spectrum, there are still more than a few members who don’t have body guys and view them as unnecessary. Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-North Dakota) believes that having someone shadow him would be a “waste of time” for one or both of them.

“I’m not that insecure,” Cramer told NOTUS. “I detest that part of it, and anybody on my staff will tell you so. Having to have somebody hover around me and tell me what to do. I carry two phones. I’m easy to communicate with. If I’m not communicating back, it’s because I don’t want to. I keep pretty close track of the issues. … I don’t need that security blanket.”

“Politics does sort of breed a sort of insecurity in people. I think insecurity goes hand in hand with ego. I just don’t like it,” Cramer continued. “I do not need somebody for the sake of being there.”

Others believe that their decision to navigate the hallways solo fits with their general disposition. Sen. Cynthia Lummis (R-Wyoming) pointed to her Western upbringing and past life as a rancher, along with her need for “more alone time.”

“I'd rather be alone, not have a tagalong. I'm also one of those people who has personal space, and I know that I need more personal space than a lot of Easterners do,” she said in an interview. “I just need more personal space. I need more alone time.”

Some body people are there to physically support their aging bosses. The late Mississippi Sen. Thad Cochran was often so disoriented in the Capitol building, he required several body people to make sure he ended up in the right place. He once went into a room where Democrats were meeting for lunch and stayed there until someone asked if he was planning on eating with Democrats. Eventually his body man, who had lost track of him temporarily, ferried him away to the GOP room.

During busy voting days, body men tend to congregate outside the Senate chamber, waiting to accompany their boss to their next appointment. Their presence can contribute to crowding in the tight hallways, especially when dozens of reporters are doing the same.

"Every senator does not need a body man. These are emotional support body men," one Senate reporter griped to NOTUS.

But senior Hill aides said that body people play an important role in keeping their boss on schedule. They are circumspect when hiring for the role because it includes access to private conversations.

“You need someone who is reliable and discreet,” said a chief of staff for a Republican senator. “They’re in the car with the senator, in meetings with them and hear them on the phone.”

Chris Marroletti, a former body man for retired Utah Sen. Mitt Romney, said a successful body person helps anticipate challenges and maintains a high standard of professionalism, no matter what situation may arise.
Mitt Romney (3200x2133, AR: 1.50)“They could be having a personal family emergency, and you're in the car and have to be there. You can't jump out of the limo or something,” Marroletti said. “You are quite literally connected with them. You’re the first person that they see at work and the last person they see at night before they talk to their spouse.”

Maroletti, who was known by friends as the chair of the Body Guy Caucus during his time on Capitol Hill, now runs an unofficial school for wannabe bodies.

Other former body people described the experience as challenging yet rewarding, and one that fosters camaraderie in what is otherwise a highly polarized environment on Capitol Hill.

“It’s one of the most special parts of the Senate because that culture does not exist in the House,” said one Republican operative who used to shadow a senator. “I think as a whole if Congress worked a little more like the Body Guy Caucus, I think we'd be in a little bit of a better place.”

Photo credits: Francis Chung/POLITICO via AP; Mariam Zuhaib/AP; Igor Bobic/NOTUS
entries.author: Igor Bobic, Al Weaver, Reese Gorman

entries.title: After a Summer of Uncertainty and Panic, a Howard Freshman Moves In
entries.summary: Faith Ngwa was one of 200 students who briefly lost their spots in Howard’s freshman class.
entries.content:
Faith Ngwa woke up early to make the 90-minute drive from her home in Hagerstown, Maryland, to the campus of Howard University. She arrived promptly at 8 a.m. and was soon greeted by the one thing every student hopes to see on their college move-in day: a familiar face. Talking to an upperclassman she knew through a friend, conversation inevitably turned to the news of the summer.

“I’m so happy things worked out,” the elder student said.

Weeks before move-in day, it was unclear if Ngwa would have a spot at The Mecca. She had long wanted to attend Howard, one of the nation’s preeminent historically Black universities. In April, her phone flooded with congratulatory messages after she posted that she was going to be a Bison.

But that dream appeared to be dashed in late July, when Ngwa discovered she was one of 502 students who were unenrolled from Howard after failing to meet payment deadlines. Following a social media firestorm, about 200 of them — including Ngwa — were reenrolled. It was a whirlwind experience, lasting just a week, but it was still on her mind as she made her way to Howard’s Northwest D.C. campus for a Friday morning move-in.

The scene was crowded but orderly. Upperclassmen went car to car, providing the freshman and their families with a cart or a helping hand. As Ngwa wrapped up her conversation with her friend, her family members, who drove down in another car, began assessing how they were going to unload. They had brought all of the dorm room staples: mini fridge, clothes, trash can, sheets, hangers, a large pink mirror. In her own car, Ngwa had snacks and toiletries.
DSC04170_toned.jpg (3000x2000, AR: 1.50)Her sister, Lois Ngam, stood in front of a cart brimming over with lamps, dorm accessories and a suitcase, shaking her head. She was still worried, thinking back to the moment her sister lost her place at Howard shortly after purchasing many of these supplies.

“It was just like, ‘What is going on?’” Ngam recalled. “Is this going to be an every-semester thing? Or is it just the first semester? It's just kind of uncertain.”

The pink mirror was loaded into the cart last and Ngwa’s family made their way toward the dorm. They passed other freshmen with their parents, siblings, cousins and friends — everyone scrambling around the campus, working hard to get these new Bison settled.

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Looking for Answers

On July 22, news of Howard’s mass unenrollment started to trickle into social media feeds. Some of the affected students made video testimonials, many saying they had been wronged by the school they had been planning to attend in less than a month.

Days later, the university confirmed that it had unenrolled 502 students, saying that even after “multiple communications and deadline extensions” these students “had not satisfied the University's enrollment requirements.” At that point, the online discourse took off. Posts were made, debates were had, students were interviewed.

Ngwa posted her own video that week describing her situation. In early July, she had started receiving notices about registration holds placed on her account. Federal loans she’d taken out remained pending on the school’s financial aid portal, and she wasn’t sure why.

She called the school’s financial aid office and received a surprisingly casual response.

“[The person who picked up is] just living her best life and says, ‘Yep, you’re good. You don’t have to worry about it,’” she said in her video. “But that doesn’t make sense because on my [portal], it’s still saying past due.”
Howard University Students Unenrolled (8041x5361, AR: 1.50)When Ngwa got the email saying she was no longer a member of the class of 2030, she was devastated. Coming from a Cameroonian-American family, she viewed the university as a “once in a lifetime opportunity” and had already started planning out the next four years. She wanted to major in communications. She wanted to take part in the school’s famous homecoming celebrations. She wanted to study abroad in Brazil. She wanted the full Howard experience.

So she went looking for answers.

“The amount of emails I sent, let's just say I wasn't really nice,” Ngwa recalled. “I was typing out of emotion.”

She emailed the school’s bursar. She emailed the financial aid office. She panicked. She considered driving down to D.C. to try and get some answers in person, but her family encouraged her to remain calm. Things will work out, they said

Days later, Ngwa’s online account updated and she was officially reenrolled.

In a statement issued July 30, interim President Wayne A. I. Frederick wrote that each of the 502 student accounts affected had been reexamined. The Washington Post later reported that roughly 200 of those 502 students were reinstated.

When contacted by NOTUS, a Howard spokesperson said the school does not comment on individual student accounts but pointed to Frederick’s statement.

‘Truth and Service’ 


On a warm Sunday evening two days after move-in, Howard’s incoming freshmen filtered into the university’s football stadium to take the final symbolic step toward becoming Bison: the pinning ceremony. It’s a tradition that has grown in scale over the years, where members of the new class get a small pin featuring Howard’s insignia and motto: “Veritas et Utilitas.” Truth and service.

The sun began to set as the freshmen, donned in white, filled the bleachers on one side of the stadium field. Thousands of parents, siblings and other family members packed bleachers on the opposite side and the field.

Ngwa had spent the weekend getting acclimated to her new living space. She and her roommate, Meonna Acree, had become fast friends. Acree had also been unenrolled and reenrolled last month. They walked around together, wearing dresses they had bought specifically for the pinning ceremony. Ngwa walked gingerly. She had injured her leg at some point over the weekend, but decided to wear heels anyway.

“Beauty is pain,” she said.

As the ceremony began, student leaders riled up the freshmen, encouraging them to yell in response to their dorms being called out — Annex, College Hall North, the Quad. A small section of freshmen screamed in excitement as the musician Usher walked past; he was there to see his son join the class of 2030.

One parent in the crowd, who asked to remain anonymous in order to candidly discuss Howard’s enrollment process, said she had mixed emotions being at the pinning ceremony. Her daughter had narrowly avoided disenrollment over the summer after a miscommunication about payments.

“My child turned down quite a few other schools because she wanted to be here,” she said. “Some of these kids, [financial aid] is their only way in. [Howard] needs to be more transparent with everything.”

As celebratory music began playing, she looked out over the crowd of proud parents in Howard gear.
DSC04150 copy.jpg (3250x2206, AR: 1.47)“I’m happy to be here. But I’m a little upset thinking to myself, ‘There are parents that should have been here who are not here.’ I’m fortunate enough to be here but I could’ve been one of those parents. I know that [unenrollment] would’ve devastated my child because she wouldn't have come back the next year. I would not have allowed her to.”

Students, alumni and administrative leaders spoke one after the other. They talked about tradition and growth. They joked about the school’s rivalry with Hampton University. They used words like “legacy” and “becoming.”

“Remember, Howard chose you,” one speaker said.

But there was no acknowledgement of the experience 200 of the freshmen had gone through. Nor was there a mention of the 300 students who were missing from the ceremony.

“Everybody has no choice but to move on, despite what has happened,” Ngwa said later. “But it's like at some point, the administration has to mention it and learn from it in order for this to not happen again.”
DSC04129_toned.jpg (3000x2000, AR: 1.50)She was already looking forward to the week following the pinning ceremony. “Bison Week” is filled with activities: A D.C. night tour where students would bring boomboxes to dance in front of the Lincoln Memorial. Information sessions on study abroad. A “Taste of Howard” event in the yard, where members of the Greek organizations would stroll and step, introducing the students to the true HBCU experience.

“I'm very excited,” she said. “I do want to run for a lot of things, join a lot of organizations because hey, if Howard has already stressed me out this much, I might as well take full advantage.”

At the end of Sunday night, when relatives were encouraged to find their Bison and help them affix the pin to their lapel or dress, Ngwa’s family got caught up in the crowd. She believes they “weren’t really understanding the assignment” and were trying to get a photo of Usher.

“So I had to pin myself,” she said. “But that’s okay. I got a pin.”

entries.title: Supreme Court Again Rebuffs Trump’s Effort to Appeal E. Jean Carroll Payout
entries.summary: This is the second time Trump asked the Supreme Court to consider his appeal.
entries.content:
The Supreme Court declined Monday to consider President Donald Trump’s attempt to overturn the $5 million verdict from a jury that found he sexually abused the writer E. Jean Carroll in the 1990s and later defamed her.

This is the second time Trump asked the Supreme Court to consider his appeal. The president will have to pay the more than $5 million in damages he owes Carroll stemming from a 2023 civil trial that found him liable for sexual abuse and defamation.

The high court denied Trump’s request — along with a list of other cases — as part of its scheduled “summer order lists.” The justices did not provide any explanation for why they declined to take up Trump’s appeal, which is consistent with Supreme Court practice.

Trump had asked the Supreme Court to reconsider his appeal because it's connected to a judgment of $83 million against the president in a separate defamation case filed by Carroll. Trump petitioned the Supreme Court to toss out that judgment as well, and that case remains pending.

The smaller $5 million judgement resulted from a lawsuit Carroll filed in 2022. The columnist alleged Trump sexually assaulted her in a Bergdorf Goodman dressing room in 1996 and detailed the incident in her 2019 memoir. Trump has vigorously denied the accusation, telling a reporter from The Hill in 2019 that “she’s not my type.”

Trump has now exhausted his appeals in this case, and lawyers for Carroll told The Associated Press she had collected the full judgement last month.

“The Eagle has landed,” Carroll wrote on X, shortly after the news broke that she received the compensatory damages.

In a court filing submitted after the Supreme Court issued its first rejection of the president’s appeal on June 29, Carroll’s lawyers argued that Trump had hindered payment by “slow-roll[ing] his defenses, asserting or inventing a new one each time his prior effort to delay the case fails.”

Trump maintains that Carroll falsified the accusation.

“I’ve never met this person in my life,” Trump said in a statement in 2019. “She is trying to sell a new book; that should indicate her motivation. It should be sold in the fiction section.”
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: UK Prime Minister Texted With a Susie Wiles Impersonator
entries.summary: The incident comes a year after federal authorities launched an investigation into a hack targeting Wiles’ phone.
entries.content:
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham exchanged messages earlier this year with an unknown individual pretending to be White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, a White House official confirmed on Monday.

The incident, first reported by Politico, comes a year after President Donald Trump’s administration launched an investigation into a hack targeting Wiles’ phone.

“We do not comment on national security matters,” Downing Street told NOTUS. One person briefed on the communications said a “few messages” were exchanged after Burnham assumed office but insisted they were “of no significance,” according to Politico.

Shortly after Trump returned to the White House last year, lawmakers and other top administration officials began to receive messages from someone who appeared to be impersonating Wiles. Federal officials launched an investigation and informed Wiles that contacts in her personal cellphone had been hacked, according to a report from The Wall Street Journal at the time.

But the White House insists that this incident is unrelated to that breach.

“This incident had nothing to do with the Chief of Staff’s devices being hacked,” a White House official told NOTUS.

The most recent subterfuge was discovered after Burnham became suspicious that the messages were illegitimate, and the British embassy in Washington flagged the incident with the White House, according to Politico.

The nature and substance of the messages exchanged between Burnham and the impersonator remains unclear.

Wiles has been one of Trump’s top advisers since the start of his second term. Prior to joining Trump’s presidential campaign in 2023, Wiles was a prominent Republican strategist and lobbyist. She is the first woman to serve as the White House chief of staff.

Burnham was sworn in as Prime Minister on July 20, after winning a special election to parliament in June. Burnham is a member of the Labour Party, a major center-left political party in the U.K. He replaced former Prime Minister Keir Starmer, who had resigned.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin
